But the order states the correction window as 'a reasonable time' when the statute says twenty-four hours, and it omits the required follow-up written report to the supervisor. second_check.explanation: The finding holds. I read the version of R.C. 4113.52(A)(1)(a) in effect 4-6-2023, the version that applies to the 2023 conduct. It requires the employee to "orally ... notify" the supervisor and "subsequently shall file with that supervisor or officer a written report." The employer then has a fixed window: "If the employer does not correct the violation or make a reasonable and good faith effort to correct the violation within twenty-four hours after the oral notification or the receipt of the report, whichever is earlier..." The order instead says the employee must "allow a reasonable time for the employer to correct," and it leaves out the written-report step. That is a different rule from the statute, not a paraphrase of it. The order also presents (A)(1)(a) as a general prerequisite. In fact (A)(1)(a) applies only to violations the employee reasonably believes are criminal offenses likely to cause imminent harm, felonies, or improper solicitations, and (A)(2) allows direct agency reporting of criminal violations of Chapters 3704, 3734, 6109 and 6111. Oral notice to a supervisor is a real prerequisite, so the authority partly supports the order. But the correction-period and written-report elements are misstated, and those are exactly what a jury instruction would turn on.
